content: Mimosine is an alkaloid and a β-3-hydroxy-4-pyridone amino acid. It is a toxic, non-proteinogenic amino acid that is chemically similar to tyrosine. Mimosine was first isolated from Mimosa pudica. In ruminants, mimosine is metabolized into 3,4-dihydroxypyridone (3,4-DHP) and 2,3-dihydroxypyridone (2,3-DHP). This compound is found in a few other species of the Mimosa genus and in all members of the closely related genus Leucaena. Cases of mimosine toxicity have been reported in regions such as Australia, Papua New Guinea, Africa, and Florida. However, no such cases have been documented in other tropical and subtropical areas. In Myanmar, goats experienced hair loss when their diet consisted of 50% Leucaena. In contrast, goats and cattle in Hawaii are capable of degrading 3,4-DHP in their rumen. This tolerance to mimosine and its metabolites may depend on the presence or absence of specific microbes that can metabolize mimosine and 3,4-DHP. It has been observed that Australian goats lack the ability to metabolize mimosine as effectively as their Hawaiian counterparts. The initial bacterial population used for inoculation was not a pure culture. From this mixed culture, pure bacterial colonies capable of degrading both isomers of DHP (3,4-DHP and 2,3-DHP) were successfully isolated. One such strain, initially named strain 78-1 (ATCC 49833), is strictly anaerobic during growth. It can be stored at 20°C and tolerates temperatures up to 50°C, beyond which it is no longer viable. The substrates these bacteria ferment, their cell wall composition, and their rRNA sequences indicate that they are not closely related to any other known rumen bacteria. In 1992, a bacterial strain capable of degrading mimosine was named in honor of R.J. Jones. Additionally, Aung from Myanmar identified new bacteria with the ability to degrade mimosine. Attempts to transfer rumen liquor from goats to sheep in India, in an effort to improve mimosine metabolism in sheep, have been unsuccessful.
